To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) Bayesian models can explain differences in the performance of machine learning methods on EEG and fNIRS data in different conditions, (b) these models posit that the brain organizes calculations on two anti- correlated networks, one that minimizes surprise and the other that maximizes surprise, and (c) these models can be used to design Bidirectional BCIs that optimize user state by modulating the flow of information to a user’s brain in a feedback loop

we have developed new methods for implicit BCIs based on Bayesian and systems neuroscience models of brain function and have shown that these methods can be used to design a new type of BCI that optimizes the user’s state.

we show how Bayesian and neural network models of the brain explain differences in performance of machine-learning algorithms trained on brain activity in different conditions, and that we propose a new type of brain-computer interface that uses information theory to optimize the flow of information to and from the user.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to design BCIs that use brain measurements of the user’s attentional state to adaptively optimize the flow of information to that user.
the design of new types of BCIs that use information theoretical measures of the user to optimize the user experience.
how to measure the user’s brain state in a way that allows for a better user experience and how to use this measurement to optimize the digital flow of sensory information to the user.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Entropic BCI is a type of Bidrectional BCI, which uses physiological measures to evaluate the digital information flow to the brain, which can be tweaked in a feedback loop for the user's benefit.
we propose a new type of BCI, which we call Entropic BCI that is based on the user’s attentional state.
the brain is a probabilistic system, which is a system that is based on probability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is an information processing device and we can leverage this knowledge for better human-computer interactions.
we show how the brain can be used to improve the user’s state, and how to measure this state using fNIRS and how to use these measures to drive a BCI.
the brain is a Bayesian machine that aims to minimize the surprisal of the world around it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain’s internal calculations can be understood as an information-theoretic process, and that the information-theoretic state of the brain can be measured and used as a control signal for BCI.
the information theoretic properties of the user’s brain state can be used to drive implicit BCIs.

we have shown how to use a new class of machine learning algorithms to extract the information content of brain signals and use them as a basis for designing new BCI’s that aim to improve the state of the user.
